title: Tenali Raman Tale 144

full_text:
An elderly scholar named Ramakrishna Shastri purchased a fine, hand-woven Benares silk turban dyed with rare vegetable indigo, embroidered with tiny silver lotus motifs along the border.
While taking a bath at the public river ghat, he left the turban on a flat stone.
A haughty courtier named Somappa snatched the turban and wrapped it around his own head.
When the poor scholar confronted him, Somappa sneered:
'Old beggar! This turban is an ancestral heirloom of my noble family! How dare a threadbare scholar claim my silk?'

The dispute was brought before Tenali Raman.
Somappa produced three friends who swore the turban had belonged to his family for years.
The poor scholar wept, having no witnesses.

Tenali Raman looked at the disputed silk turban.
He asked Somappa: 'What thread was used to stitch the inner lining of this turban?'
Somappa guessed: 'Fine silver thread, of course!'
Tenali asked the scholar: 'What thread was used?'
The scholar answered:
'Because I am poor, my wife stitched the inner headband with coarse, blue cotton thread, and inside the seam she placed a small dried jasmine leaf for fragrance.'

Tenali carefully snipped two stitches of the inner lining before the court:
Inside was coarse blue cotton thread, and between the silk folds lay a single, dried, fragrant jasmine leaf!

Tenali smiled:
'Somappa, you know the price of silk, but only the poor scholar’s wife knows the humble thread that binds it!'

Somappa was fined fifty gold coins for theft and perjury, which were awarded to the scholar, and the silk turban was restored to its rightful owner.
The court praised Tenali Raman’s gentle, observant justice.
moral: Careful examination of the smallest details exposes the claims of arrogant thieves.
